p: So the funding is actually considered public housing program income, and by HUD rules, we're required to provide it back to the development in the same way that we would rent. So we're not allowed to give it to the tenants.
How do it go back to the tenants?
It has to go back to the budget of that particular development. So every—
To do what? I just want to know-

To support the operating budget— so it could be to support the contracts, the personnel. It's not a significant amount of money, but every dollar that we collect at that development has to go back to the budget at that development per the HUD rules.
So just to upgrade that development, not to give to the constituents of that development. Since the TA did give y'all authorization, is there any way it could go back to the people?
It cannot go to the tenant association by the HUD rules. It has to go back to the development budget overall, which would benefit the residents.
Could you tell me one benefit?
It supports the normal operating budget of the development, so it helps to pay for the staffing, the contracts, in the same way that rent does, in the same way that—
So, could you hire one of the constituents or one of the TA or one of their board members that they could see tangible?
We have a full Section 3 program where we do hire our public housing residents, which we’re happy to discuss.
Okay.
Could we do something on Section 3 to see how many of the constituents of NYCHA is really getting these jobs?
Yes, I'll oblige to that.
Have a breakdown of the jobs that NYCHA— and I'm done. Thank you.
We'll allow another round for you, uh, Council Member Mealy, if you— okay.
He was about to give it to me.
Uh, Council Member Marte.
Thank you.
You're welcome.

Um, earlier today you mentioned that, um, you're looking at other properties to do demolition. What are some of those other properties that, um, you have classified need demolition in your perspective?

Well, as I said, we're not— we're not— we don't identify sites and think this is a site for demolition, right? What we do is we prioritize the sites that need investment, and we go and we start talking to residents about, A, the need, what we understand the need to be through the

physical needs assessment that Shaan described earlier, and we hear from them what they think the needs are, and we talk about the range of options, which could be preservation through conventional PACT preservation, or it could be some combination of preservation with new construction. So we don't go in assuming a demolition. It is what can we do to invest in this community.
From your active conversations, um, can you tell us which developments, um, have had that conversation of potential demolition and, um, and ones that might be— you might be interested in pursuing?
Right now, the only other development that is considering new construction, um, is Meltzer.

Okay. The- Meltzer- he said, just making it clear. Um, you know, every agency was assigned a Chief Savings Officer, and a report was due a few days ago. Uh, when can that, or when do you estimate that report is going to be public knowledge? Um, to, yeah, for the Council to see.

Since our Chief Savings Officer has, uh, stepped away for a minute, if we can - we'll stick a pin in that and, uh, she can respond to that when she's back because I'm unsure and I don't want to misspeak.
Yeah. Are there any major potential saving mechanisms, uh, that NYCHA is pursuing as part of this report, uh, that the mayor required that you can share with us today?

I can say that when we were preparing our 2026 budget under the backdrop of knowing that we would have significant, uh, a significant decrease in our federal funding, we really took a hard look at, um, our individual budgets and we were able to find, uh, about $100 million worth of savings. Now that savings, uh, based on our- our federal funding, uh, the operating funding that we get from the city is really— because we're not a city agency— is minimal. So the savings that we realized, and which allowed us to go into 2026 with a balanced budget, um, is different than the savings exercise that, uh, the city asked us to go through.

Okay. Um, okay. Um, since, uh, just going back to, uh, you mentioned Meltzer, um, I know during the Bloomberg Administration there was plans for a next-gen development in Meltzer. Is this re-adopting that proposal, or is this a new proposal, uh, that you had conversation with, with the tenant association there?

As I understand the Bloomberg proposal, it was meant to be an infill, uh, 80% market, 20% affordable on the vacant, uh, er, on the, the, um, you know, the park space essentially. Um, while then using the proceeds from that transaction to rehabilitate the existing development. So that's what that was. Um, but that's not what we're talking about. What the residents of Meltzer has said— have said is that they want a brand new building for themselves. So we have ju— like, they have actually just made that determination last week. They very affirmatively said in front of the elected officials and others that they would like a new building at Meltzer. So that's part 1, and then we will think about what to do with the existing building.
Okay, I have no further questions, Chair.

Thank you. Council Member Elsie. COUNCIL MEMBER ENCARNACIÓN: I thought you were gonna do it again. You did good the last time. Um, so, uh, we mentioned, uh, well, you guys mentioned that you had 464 full-time vacant positions. Um, How many of those are maintenance positions?

So, in truth, I don't have it by maintenance, but I can tell you that, um, at the properties and borough offices, there are 64 full-time positions that are vacant. In our operations support services, there's 203, and in our central office departments, it's 197. But I don't have it by maintenance workers specifically. COUNCIL MEMBER ENCARNACIÓN: Okay, and, and in consideration of that, if a development was to lose, um, some, uh, maintenance workers, she does have it. Oh, beautiful.

Yeah, it's pretty small. Mhm. So the maintenance workers, they must be really small because they're not on my list.

COUNCIL MEMBER ENCARNACIÓN: Okay, so really, really small, but if a development were to lose maintenance workers, we do shift around maintenance workers, so there's equity, equity across the system in terms of a development not having one and another development having 3. I don't know.

Yes, thank you, Council Member. I wanna also add that our— while it seems like a lot, our time to fill frontline positions is about 30 days right now, so we are able - we are working well to rehire once we have a true vacancy, but if there is a significant situation where we have a vacancy and we need support, we are able to shift from other properties on a temporary basis in order to get— make sure that we have coverage, um, while we are going through that hiring process. COUNCIL MEMBER ENCARNACIÓN: And is that determined by the size of the development, how many maintenance workers they receive?

Yes. COUNCIL MEMBER ENCARNACIÓN: Yes, okay. Um, and then typically, so wait, let me go back. So I wanna talk about some of the delays in the capital projects. I know you said that it takes about 4 to 5

years for capital projects to be completed, and that's if nothing else interferes, I'm assuming. Um, but, you know, for example, there are developments in my district that experience high levels of public safety concerns, right? Um, we may put in money for security cameras. That project might go really, really quickly. However, the true determinants, uh, of crime, or what we really need to address are things like community centers. And even when they're fully funded, they take a really long time to get through. Now, I know that that's a bigger project than a camera being installed, but I'm trying to understand the prioritization. I mean, we have a community center that's been on hold since the de Blasio days. It's really affecting the quality of life and the safety of our residents when we can't provide those resources. So I'm just trying to get to where that delay is when it comes to bigger projects. Is there enough staff? Is there- you know what happens there.

Great, thank you for the question. Um, and I know, uh, across the 23 developments you have, there, there are many

different ongoing projects and ongoing needs. You're right, projects like CCTV move much quicker— more quickly than other types of projects given the specific scope of work. Community centers in particular are, um, quite complex because they involve so many different trades. However, in terms of your question around prioritization, as soon as we have funding available, we move projects very quickly. There's no prioritization or lag that a certain type of project moves quicker than another. Um, we typically maintain sufficient resourcing to be able to ensure that there isn't a gap between when funding's available to us and we can initiate a project. Often we even staff a team before the funding is fully available. Once we know it's secured and it's coming, we'll start engagement on the site and then we move the project quickly. So the, the real, uh, constraint on some of the community centers that you may be thinking about is that we don't have funding for renovation there. And that comes back to a broader question of how we prioritize our capital funding. The vast majority—

COUNCIL MEMBER ENCARNACIÓN: Well, specifically, I was talking about Wagner, if, if you wanted to look it up, and that funding was complete. I'm sure after all of these years, it probably needs more funding now, which is a problem because when things take a long time to get, you know, once they're fully funded, if they don't move, then we end up having to pay more money, um, because costs go up every year.

Yes. Um, so I can come back to you with the specific details on Wagner. Um, we do provide, uh, on any active projects that's publicly available on our website, the initial schedule of the project, where exactly we are today, um, what is the forecast schedule, if there have been any delays. Um, and then we also provide a- a biannual summary letter to all Council Members of all projects in their district, including those that are council-funded and those that are funded from any other source that provides the same level of detail of what's happening in each project. So I can follow up and, um, if you have not seen that recent biannual letter that we've sent, we can send that again. And that would not only provide the

details on Wagner, but all of the projects in your district. COUNCIL MEMBER ENCARNACIÓN: Yeah, Okay. Um, and then typically when a building fails inspection, uh, regular building, not a NYCHA building, when they fail an inspection, they usually get a fine um, or something. What happens with NYCHA when there's an inspection failed, when there's mold or lead, or like, what is the process there? I don't know.

Thank you. Can you clarify what kind of inspection you're referring to? COUNCIL MEMBER ENCARNACIÓN: A building inspection. So when a regular HPD building gets inspected for— a 311 triggers an inspection from the Department of Buildings, there's an accountability measure. There's a fine that's assessed if they are out of compliance. I'm just trying to figure out what the accountability measure is if NYCHA's doing their own inspections, finding things, like, what, what happens?

Yeah, so, um, NYCHA buildings, uh, go through a variety of different inspections. We are required by HUD to do our own inspections every year of all apartments. And so last year we, you

know, we have to achieve over 95% of apartment inspections. In the last 2 years we were able to do so. Um, in addition, HUD does inspections of our properties every year. And so those are called our INSPIRE inspections, and those are conducted by HUD, and we work with HUD to follow up on any deficiencies found during those inspections. And then in addition, um, if residents are involved in housing court actions, HPD may come and, and they wouldn't do a whole building inspection, but they would come to the apartment and they would inspect the condition and they would issue us a violation. COUNCIL MEMBER ENCARNACIÓN: And, and, uh, fines associated with, with that ever, or did they not apply for NYCHA?
I don't— we don't get the fines. We need to follow up with HPD on all the inspections. COUNCIL MEMBER ENCARNACIÓN: And are those, uh, Inspire inspections public, the findings of those?
I, I think they may be on the HUD website. We can confirm. COUNCIL MEMBER ENCARNACIÓN: Okay, thank you. Thank you so much, Chair.

Thank you, thank you. Alright, I have some follow-up questions to the questions we gave earlier, um, and first I wanna go back, uh, to, uh, Chelsea Elliott— sorry, Fulton Elliott Chelsea. Um, wanna know directly, why has NYCHA not submitted the Fulton Elliott Chelsea application to the City Council for approval, uh, through the ULUP process, the initial process, uh, when the, I guess, the transition or the conversion was taking place?
So each of the first 2 buildings at Fulton and Chelsea addition, uh, can be built as of right and do not require
Okay. Now, following up, uh, to one of, uh, Council Member Chi Ossé’s question earlier, uh, after PACT, uh, conversion is complete, who is responsible for the building upkeep and physical need?
The development team that we have selected, so it would be the joint venture between the developer and the property manager.

'Cause I know there have been, uh, many— well, under the conversions that have been done, residents have complained and said that,

uh, in the— during that process, uh, services, uh, you know, as far as when calls are made they're not being— they're not being responded to.
So again, just to be clear, prior to the conversion, the buildings are still under NYCHA responsibility.
Under NYCHA right.

So anything that happens before the conversion should go through NYCHA. After the conversion, everything should go through the property manager. And then, as I said earlier in the hearing, if residents don't feel like they, um, are having their issues addressed, there are many venues. Again, they can reach out to the asset management team, they can call 311, they can call the CCC, they can call the, uh, ombudsman, uh, they can go through our leased housing team. So there's a lot of venues to have issues addressed if for whatever reason it's not— okay, not to their satisfaction.

Okay, I know you mentioned the, uh, satisfaction rate, uh, for the— for PACT residents. Do you have a satisfaction rate, uh, data

for the just traditional Section 9 residents? And if so, what is that rate?
We do not have that for Section 9.
So, uh, how do you, how do you gauge the residents, uh, when there are issues and complaints.
We did, we did conduct a resident survey for Section 9. I don't have the results with us right now.
So there is, there is a—
And I, I'm not sure if there was an equal—
So just provide it for the Committee.
We can follow up on the resident survey.

Okay, so if you can provide that for the Committee, we appreciate it. Um, backtracking also to, uh, the vacant unit readiness follow-up, how many NYCHA staff are focused just on the vacant, uh, unit readiness program?

So we don't have staff that are specifically focused on vacant unit readiness. What

it is, is all of our skilled trade, our lead, our abatement workers, they're all working both in occupied apartments as well as unoccupied or vacant apartments.

Okay, and, and when looking at, um, contra— uh, looking at contracted out work versus skilled trade pieces done in-house, uh, is there any general vacant unit readiness contract where vacant units come under one portfolio, or does each development have their own, own contracts?

So for the most part, I wanna say over 70% or so of our vacant units are turned over by our staff, our skilled trade teams and property management teams. We do use vendors for about 20 to 30% of the vacant units. Particularly we're focusing our vendors in areas where we have, uh, vacant unit turns in relation to our modernization programs. So since we hold vacant units offline for, uh, facilitating relocations for our, uh, upcoming trust programs, but our comprehensive modernization programs like at St. Nick's and Todt Hill, we wanna make sure residents are able to have units nearby their home development in— for that relocation time period. And so that creates a cluster of vacant

units all in one spot and so we use vendors to address those.
And so is it centralized?
That piece is centralized.
Okay. Um, are there any performance metrics in those contracts?
I'd have to check those contracts and get back to you.
And, uh, what is the total amount including federal funding for vacant unit readiness in Fiscal 2027, and, uh, how much is, uh, how much is for contracts versus in-house work?

One second. Um, so for fiscal— city fiscal year 2027, we have $14.6 million in expense funding for vacant units, and there is $59 million in capital funds for vacant units. Um, in addition to the $25 million we mentioned from the state capital. That money is technically in '26, but we are working on spending it down.
Okay, thank you. Uh, when it comes to the comprehensive modernization, uh, what developments are currently undergoing, uh, comp mod, and are residents, uh, consulted through this process?

Yes, thank you for the question, uh, Chair. So currently we have 4 active projects that are in construction um, at St. Nicholas Houses, at Todt Hill Houses in Staten Island, at Gowanus Houses, and at Wyckoff Gardens. Residents are engaged extensively, typically starting 2 years before we even get to procurement and bring on a vendor. Um, there are literally thousands of flyers. Um, there are many meetings at each site, both resident leadership as well as broader resident meetings. Um, uh, building up to, uh, deciding the scope of the work, um, putting out a procurement, um, and then bringing on a vendor. Once the vendor is brought on, throughout the design and construction phases, there are requirements for regular ongoing engagement of residents in the process.
Is that engagement— is it documented?
Yes, all of that is documented.
Can you turn it over to the Committee?

Uh, yes, and in fact, a good amount of it we put on our website, so residents at

that— those specific developments can see the materials, can see the actual engagement that's happened over the years.
And is there also a satisfaction survey for that work?

Yeah, so moving forward for all capital projects, um, last year we piloted a project-specific survey for each project that happens after the design phase and after construction. This year we're scaling that up to our whole portfolio. The citywide council of presidents actually inputted to the right questions to ask in that survey to all residents. So we are now rolling that out across all of our projects.
Can you give us some insight on, uh, what has been the feedback from the residents through those surveys?
Yeah.
And can you also then provide those surveys or that data to us?

Sure. So we'll provide the survey questions and all that with you. During the pilot phase, um, and we've surveyed both the residents and we also survey our property and staff who are

involved in the project and can give us insights on how to deliver projects better with less disruption to the property, etcetera. Um, we ask a range of questions around how they were engaged in the initial scoping, the planning, how they were engaged in it, uh, to the design process, how resident input was reflected. And then also, um, during construction, did we do the best we could to, uh, minimize disruption, to communicate about what's happening? Um, uh, and to, um, uh, involve them in the process of checking the quality of the work, things like that. Now these surveys are to the resident leadership, um, and there's a variety of questions. I can tell you that in the pilots we did, um, you know, they can rate each thing from a kind of 1 to a 5 type of scale, and typically we were getting in the ranges of 4s, um, or 4.5s on average.
That’s pretty high.

Yeah, we were, we were, um, surprised that the first time we rolled this out we had quite positive feedback, but obviously it's a small sample of projects. Uh, we're very keen to roll it out fully and really use that to, um,

continue to improve the way we engage and deliver projects.
If you can turn that over to us, we would love to verify what you're saying today.
Yeah, we can share some information from there yeah.

Thank you. Uh, I know earlier you mentioned, um, about the $1.2 billion as far as the, uh, comprehensive modernization. We wanted to know, uh, that $1.2 billion million in funding mentioned, uh, during the, uh, testimony. What's the source?

So a significant portion is coming from the city underneath our City Capital Action Plan, which is part of the HUD agreement. Um, we were able to fund the projects at St. Nicholas and Todt Hill through the Gowanus rezoning, um, funding the projects at Gowanus and Wyckoff. And more recently, we have been trying to finalize some funding from FEMA, um, for some of the sites that were affected out of the Ida storm.
Okay.

And the funding is substantial enough because they're very small sites with one

building where we can do a pretty, uh, significant renovation of the site.

And I'm backtracking back to, uh, Fulton Elliott Chelsea. I just wanna, uh, want some clarity. I want you to clarify when you said market rate units being developed, uh, subsidizing the capital costs of the development. Uh, but what happens to the additional revenue after the capital, capital costs are paid for, and does any of that flow back into NYCHA residents?

I mean, the whole financing is based on a multi-decade financing, right? So it is the rents that would be collected from the market rate, you know, are projected out a number of years, and it's - so it's not as if there's a one-time slug of money that is provided at the point that we close and then that's it. It's an ongoing stream of income that we are borrowing against, which allows us to build the buildings.
And I wanna just get this on the record. The infills that you're proposing, uh, at - or the infill that you're proposing at Chelsea - Chelsea Fulton, Fulton Elliot, are these gonna be fair market?
Well, there's a portion that would be, uh, market rate, yes.
And what's the percentage?
We are— well, our EIS studied up to about 2,500 units of market rate.
Market rate, 25— so-
2,500 units of market rate, up to 1,000 units of affordable, and then the 2,056 replacement units.
Is there a percentage of, uh, those units that will be— will go to NYCHA residents?

All 2,056 apartments will be rebuilt. So yes, 100% of the replacement— the infill, the infill. So the 1,000, uh, up to 1,000 units of affordable housing has not been programmed yet, but, um, yes, they could be made available to NYCHA residents.

Okay. And I noticed that, uh, early on we talked about the surveys. It was brought up by Council Member Marte, uh, and we've, I believe there's been a petition and it's been circulated at Chelsea Elliott where there's close to over 900 signatures, uh, of residents, uh, uh, in opposition to the demolition.

Are there any plans, uh, for the authority to finally listen, uh, to the residents of Chelsea Elliott and, uh, revisit, uh, the community engagement?

We have been listening. We've been engaging with the residents of Fulton and Elliott Chelsea since 2019. There was the working group that was launched in October of 2019 and ran through April of 2021. Um, and then when, you know, we picked our PACT partner in conjunction with the residents as part of a Resident Review Committee, uh, and they started to do their inspections and they— and we collectively started thinking about, uh, reconstruction. We had a whole other engagement process in 2023, uh, which ran for the first half of 2023. So we've been listening for 7 years and we'll continue to do that.
Is that information, uh, like, is it made public? Is there where we can review those surveys that were done?
Yeah, the results and the methodology are all on our website.
So we can review the surveys. Do we have a number of the amount of surveys that were collected?
So there were about— so what we had said was that, uh, anyone over the age of 18, uh, was eligible to fill out a survey.
Do you have a number of the amount of surveys that were collected?

So there was about 3,000 eligible people who could fill out a survey, and about 1,000 people filled out the survey. So 30%, and then of that, about, about 60% had said that they wanted new construction.

Order, order, guys, order. Just wanna get this on record. Order. Thank you. Okay. That concludes the questions we have for the authority. Um, hopefully you can stay back, uh, to hear, uh, testimony from, uh, the folks who pay your salaries. Um, and, uh, we look forward to you staying back so you can hear from the residents and really get a true survey from them. Thank you. You wanna maintain a level of decorum? Thank you.

work, we are just like any other NYCHA development. This does not mean that we need a demolition. them to recoup what they said to, um, um, receive back. All of this is nothing, like I said, but a white-collar scam fraud going on and who are the victims? Are the tenants.
